title: The DNA Feature in a Second Model
takeaway: A separately trained transformer, given its own dictionary learning run, yields a feature that fires on almost exactly the same tokens as the DNA feature (activation correlation 0.92) and pushes up the same nucleotide tokens. Their logit weights agree only weakly overall (0.46), but the disagreement lives in a large near-zero central mode that the paper hypothesizes is interference noise, while the small circled DNA-token mode is shared.
walkthrough:
Two scatter plots sit side by side. Both compare the same pair of features: the [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937, plotted on each panel's vertical axis, against B/1/3680 on each horizontal axis.

B is a second transformer, trained on the same dataset with a different random seed, and then given its own [[sparse-autoencoder]] run with identical hyperparameters. Asking whether the same feature turns up there is the paper's test of [[feature-universality]].

### The left panel: when they fire

This is [[activation-similarity]]. Each dot is one token position from the sample corpus. Its horizontal position is how strongly B/1/3680 fired there, its vertical position how strongly A/1/2937 fired.

Color comes from the [[dna-proxy]], reduced to yes/no by its sign: red means the surrounding text scores as a nucleotide sequence, blue means it does not.

The strips outside the frame are marginals — the distribution of each axis on its own, each bar split red and blue by what fraction of the points at that level are which. The note "Most probability mass is at zero" points at the break both axes carry, separating an exact-zero bucket from the ">0" range. Features are sparse, so nearly every token lands in that bucket.

The dots that do fire lie roughly along the diagonal, and the red mass sits together in the far upper right. The [[pearson-correlation]] is 0.92.

### The right panel: what they do

Here each dot is a vocabulary token, not a corpus position, and its coordinates are the two features' [[logit-weight]]s for it — how far each feature's firing pushes that token's next-token logit. This is [[logit-weight-similarity]].

There are two modes. The small red-circled one at the top right, near $0.35$ to $0.55$ on both axes, holds DNA tokens such as "AGT": both models push these up, and by similar amounts.

The large blue-circled one is centered on the origin and holds every other token, with weights small in both models and only loosely related. Its label reads "Interference Weights?", question mark included. The paper's guess ([[weight-interference]]) is that these weights are unwanted, forced by [[superposition]] rather than chosen.

That bulk dominates the count, so the overall correlation is only 0.46. The agreement the paper is pointing at is in the circled minority.

terms.definition: The DNA feature: feature number 2937 in dictionary learning run 1 on model A. It fires on long uppercase strings of A, T, C and G, and the paper says it is the only feature in that run devoted to the DNA context.

The identifier actually printed in both plot headers of this figure. It does not match the prose, which names A/1/2937; elsewhere in the paper A/1/2357 is the base64 feature. Everything else in the figure (the 0.92 correlation, B/1/3680, the DNA tokens) matches the DNA feature, so the header appears to be a typo.

Feature 3680 in dictionary learning run 1 on model B, the counterpart the paper found for the DNA feature. It was selected as the feature in B/1 whose activations correlate most highly with A/1/2937's.

The two one-layer transformers the paper compares, trained on the same dataset with different random seeds. Each has its own sparse autoencoder run, so features found in one are not tied by construction to features found in the other.
The paper's naming scheme: model (A or B), then dictionary learning run (1), then the index of the feature within that run's dictionary.
The panel comparing the two features by when they fire, one point per token position in the sampled corpus.
The panel comparing the two features by what they do, one point per vocabulary token.

For a given feature, a vector with one entry per vocabulary token, giving how much that feature's firing raises or lowers that token's next-token logit. In this one-layer model it can be read straight off the weights, without running the model.
The subtitle on each panel: the Pearson correlation of the two coordinates being plotted in that panel. On the left it is over token activations; on the right it is over per-token logit weights.
The two axes of the left panel: the scalar activation of A/1/2937 (vertical) and of B/1/3680 (horizontal) at the same token position.
The two axes of the right panel: how much A/1/2937 (vertical) and B/1/3680 (horizontal) each push up the same vocabulary token.
Points where the binarized DNA proxy says yes — the text around that token scores as a nucleotide sequence, or in the right panel the token itself is a DNA-like token.
Points where the binarized DNA proxy says no. In the left panel these are ordinary non-DNA contexts; in the right panel, the bulk of the vocabulary.

The narrow bands outside each axis. They show the distribution of that one axis alone, with each bar split into blue and red by the share of points at that level that the proxy calls DNA. Reading them tells you whether an axis on its own separates DNA from non-DNA.

An annotation in the lower left of the activation panel, pointing at the dense band sitting exactly at activation zero. It states that the overwhelming majority of tokens do not activate either feature at all.

A break in both activation axes. The exact-zero bucket is drawn as its own segment, separate from the continuous range of positive activations, so that the sparse nonzero values are not crushed against the axis.
The label on the small red circle in the right panel. AGT is a vocabulary token made of nucleotide letters; the circle gathers tokens of that kind, which both features push up strongly.
A three-letter nucleotide triplet that exists as a single token in the model's vocabulary. It stands in for the family of tokens made from A, T, C and G.

The label on the large blue ellipse in the right panel, question mark in the original. It marks the paper's hypothesis, not a measurement: that this near-zero central mode is cross-talk the model would rather not have, forced on it because features in superposition cannot all be orthogonal.

The hypothesis that the network represents more features than it has neurons by giving each a direction in activation space, at the cost that those directions cannot all be orthogonal and so leak into each other.
Hand-drawn shading over the two clusters in the right panel. They are annotations added to point at the modes; they are not fitted contours or confidence regions.
The dashed vertical and horizontal lines in the right panel, marking logit weight zero on each axis. They show that the bulk mode straddles zero in both models.

numbers.meaning: The Pearson correlation between the activations of A/1/2937 and B/1/3680, printed above the left panel. It is high because the two features fire on essentially the same token positions; the paper reports the same style of number for the Arabic feature (0.91), so this is the level of agreement it treats as a match.

The Pearson correlation between the two features' logit weight vectors, printed above the right panel. It is far below 0.92 because the correlation is computed over all vocabulary tokens, and the near-zero central mode contributes most of them while agreeing only loosely between the two models.
The range of both activation axes in the left panel. Activations are ReLU outputs, so they are non-negative; roughly 11 is the largest value either feature reaches on the sampled data.

The approximate activation level above which the left panel is dominated by red. The paper reports separately that all ten random dataset examples above activation 6.0 for this feature are DNA sequences, so the red concentration in the upper right is consistent with that.
The range of both logit weight axes in the right panel. Logit weights are signed: positive means the feature pushes that token up, negative means it pushes it down.

Where the circled DNA-token cluster sits on both axes. The value is read off the plot, not stated in the text; the point is that these weights are several times larger than the bulk and positive in both models at once.
The span of the dense central mode on both axes. These are the weights the paper suspects are interference: small, centered on zero, and only weakly aligned between the two models.

Context, not in this figure: the Pearson correlation between the binarized DNA proxy and A/1/2937's activations, reported in the specificity section. It is the basis for treating red-vs-blue coloring here as a reasonable stand-in for whether the context really is DNA.

Context: the number of tokens over which the paper defines activation correlation when searching another run for a feature's counterpart. B/1/3680 was chosen as the highest-correlating feature over a sample of that size.

Context from the global universality analysis: matching every A/1 feature to its best B/1 counterpart gives a median activation correlation of 0.72, while matching neurons between the same two transformers gives 0.46. The 0.92 here is well above the feature median, so this pair is a good case rather than a typical one. Note the coincidence that the neuron median equals this figure's logit weight correlation; they measure different things.

Context: the Arabic script feature's activation correlation and logit weight correlation between the same two runs. The same gap appears there, which is why the paper treats the low logit weight correlation as a property of the measure rather than a failure of this particular match.

The dictionary learning run index. Runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient; run 1 is the one used for the individual feature case studies throughout the paper, and both sides of this comparison use it so the hyperparameters match.
